notes.title: Start here: an order system rebuilt around one consistent order
notes.body:
This repo is a Java 17 command-line order management system: customers, products, orders, order lines, discounts and a status workflow, saved to a data directory. It is a reworked version of an earlier beginner project, and the course in astraupskill/ explains what was wrong with the original and how the current code prevents it.

The code lives under src/oms:

- **domain/** - Customer, Product, Order, OrderItem, OrderStatus and DomainValues (shared text and money rules).
- **service/** - CustomerService, ProductService and OrderService.
- **persistence/** - FileDataStore, StoreSnapshot and DelimitedFileUtil.
- **App** - the numbered menu.

Read astraupskill/ in this order: README, 01-CODEBASE-MAP, 02-CONCEPTS, 03-WORKED-CHANGE, 04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING. Do the trace lab (07) yourself before opening its collected answers. The 35 regression tests compile and run with plain javac and java; 04 shows the commands, and data/sample has a small dataset to copy.

excerpts.quote: This Java CLI teaches CRUD through customers, products, orders, line items, discounts, and status transitions.
java -cp out oms.RegressionTests

readMore.why: Describes the sample dataset you can copy and run the app against.

notes.title: Core idea: the order and its lines change as one unit
notes.body:
An aggregate is a group of values whose rules must hold together. Here that group is one Order: its lines, their quantities and captured prices, the discount, the status and the timestamps. A change to one of them can break a rule about another, so the code routes every change through Order itself.

Open Order.java and make a table with one row per public method that changes something (adding or merging a line, setting a quantity, removing a line, setting the discount, changing status). For each row write: which status checks run, which other values are checked, what is changed, and whether the update time moves. Then open OrderService and note, for the same commands, which checks the service adds before calling Order.

Finally, look at what every read hands back: findById, listOrders, getItems. Ask, for each, whether the caller receives the stored object or something else, and what that means for code that tries to change it.

notes.title: Core idea: one snapshot file and a careful startup
notes.body:
All data is saved to one file, oms.snapshot.txt, in the chosen directory. Each line starts with a tag: C for a customer, P for a product, O for an order's own fields and I for one order line. A header line comes first and a count line comes last. DelimitedFileUtil escapes field separators so names cannot break a line.

Read FileDataStore.load and parseRows and answer:

- Where are I rows collected, and at what point are they joined to their O row?
- When there is no snapshot file, what does the loader look for instead, and which combinations does it accept?

Then read the App constructor and main, and trace what happens when load throws: what is printed, and what the process does next. Finally read run, saveNow and exitApplication and list every path that writes the file. 04-TESTING-AND-DEBUGGING has a short section on scripting the CLI that is worth reading before you pipe input into it.

notes.title: Why the saved discount now survives a restart
notes.body:
**Key: subtotal 20.00, discount 5.00 and total 15.00, all as they were before.**

parseRows first collects every row: O rows by order id and I rows grouped by order id. Only then does it call Order.restore once per order with the complete item list. The private constructor adds all items, then validates the saved discount against the full 20.00 subtotal, so 5.00 is accepted as stored. The regression test "saved discount survives full order reload" checks 5.00 and 15.00.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Discount 0.00, total 20.00**: that was the original bug, when the order was built with no items and the discount was clamped. The fixed loader never builds that partial order.
- **Total 20.00 with discount 5.00**: totals are derived (subtotal minus discount), not cached, so they always agree.
- **Startup stops**: a 5.00 discount on a 20.00 subtotal is valid, so restore accepts it.

excerpts.quote: orders.add(Order.restore(
Because subtotal was temporarily zero, the discount became zero.

notes.title: Why a quantity cut below the discount is refused
notes.body:
**Key: refused, so quantity stays 3, discount 25.00 and total 5.00.**

setItemQuantity builds a candidate line with the new quantity and the existing name and price, works out the proposed subtotal (30.00 - 30.00 + 20.00 = 20.00) and calls validateSubtotal. A 25.00 discount is larger, so it throws "Reduce the discount before reducing the subtotal." before items.set or touch run. The user must lower the discount first. A probe confirms quantity 3 and total 5.00 afterwards.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Discount lowered to 20.00**: the code no longer changes a discount as a side effect; 02-CONCEPTS says so directly.
- **Total -5.00**: the invariant is that discount never exceeds subtotal, so a negative total is impossible.
- **Discount cleared**: nothing touches the discount in setItemQuantity.

excerpts.quote: if (discountAmount.compareTo(subtotal) > 0) throw new IllegalArgumentException("Reduce the discount before reducing the subtotal.");
the application no longer silently changes a discount as a side effect of recalculation

notes.title: Why a paid order refuses a new discount
notes.body:
**Key: "Could not apply discount: Orders in PAID status cannot be edited."**

OrderService.applyDiscount calls ensureEditable before calling Order.setDiscountAmount, and Order also checks again. isEditable returns true only for DRAFT and SUBMITTED, so a PAID order is refused with "Orders in PAID status cannot be edited." App prints its "Could not apply discount: " prefix. A probe returns that message.

Why the others are wrong:
- **"Discount applied."**: content edits stop once an order is paid; this was one of the original defects that the rework fixed.
- **"Discount cannot exceed subtotal."**: 1.00 is below the subtotal, and the status check runs first anyway.
- **A status transition message**: applying a discount is not a status change; transitions are only checked by updateStatus and setStatus.

excerpts.quote: public boolean isEditable() { return status == OrderStatus.DRAFT || status == OrderStatus.SUBMITTED; }
ensureEditable(order);

notes.title: Why changing a returned line changes nothing stored
notes.body:
**Key: nothing stored changes, because the order and its items were both handed out as copies.**

OrderService.findById maps the stored order through Order.copy, which rebuilds it with copies of every line. getItems then maps each line through OrderItem.copy again. OrderItem is still mutable, so setQuantity(99) succeeds, but only on a throwaway copy. The service's order, its lines and its derived totals are untouched; a probe shows the stored total unchanged.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Stored total grows**: that was the original defect, when items were shared objects; both layers now copy.
- **Stored quantity changes but not the total**: totals are derived from the lines, so they could not disagree; and the stored line is not reached at all.
- **setQuantity throws**: the copy is an ordinary OrderItem; nothing marks it read-only.

excerpts.quote: public List<OrderItem> getItems() { return items.stream().map(OrderItem::copy).toList(); }
return Optional.ofNullable(ordersById.get(id)).map(Order::copy);

notes.title: Which layer refuses an empty order moving to SUBMITTED
notes.body:
**Key: "Could not update order status: An empty order cannot enter that status."**

OrderService.updateStatus checks three things: not the same status, an allowed transition, and items for PAID or SHIPPED. DRAFT to SUBMITTED passes all three. It then calls Order.setStatus, which uses requiresItems, and that includes SUBMITTED. So the domain throws its own wording. A probe returns exactly this text.

Why the others are wrong:
- **"Order status updated."**: the delivered Order requires items for SUBMITTED, PAID and SHIPPED.
- **"cannot be moved to SUBMITTED"**: that is the service's wording, and its check only names PAID and SHIPPED.
- **Invalid transition**: DRAFT to SUBMITTED is in the transition table.

excerpts.quote: if (requiresItems(target) && !hasItems()) throw new IllegalArgumentException("An empty order cannot enter that status.");
if ((newStatus == OrderStatus.PAID || newStatus == OrderStatus.SHIPPED) && !order.hasItems()) {

notes.title: Why a submitted order keeps its last line
notes.body:
**Key: refused, since a submitted order must keep at least one item.**

removeItemByProductId first checks the order is editable (SUBMITTED is), finds the line, and then throws "A submitted order must keep at least one item." when the status is SUBMITTED and only one line is left. A DRAFT order can lose its last line, because empty drafts are allowed. The regression test "submitted order cannot lose its last item" checks the line is still there.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Back to DRAFT**: no code moves an order backwards; DRAFT is not reachable from SUBMITTED.
- **An empty SUBMITTED order**: SUBMITTED requires items, and this check enforces it for removal.
- **SUBMITTED not editable at all**: isEditable is true for DRAFT and SUBMITTED; quantity and discount edits still work.

excerpts.quote: if (status == OrderStatus.SUBMITTED && items.size() == 1) throw new IllegalArgumentException("A submitted order must keep at least one item.");
submitted order cannot lose its last item

notes.title: What adding the same product again does to an order
notes.body:
**Key: one notebook line of 4 units, still at its own 10.00 price snapshot.**

addOrMergeItem looks for an existing line with the same productId. It finds the notebook and calls increaseQuantity on it, which uses checked addition and recalculates that line's total from the line's own unit price. The comment says it outright: the existing line keeps its original price and name snapshot. A probe shows one line, quantity 4, unit 10.00.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Two lines**: a new line is added only when no line has that productId; the restore path even rejects duplicate product lines.
- **Replaced with 1 unit**: increaseQuantity adds; it does not overwrite.
- **Refused**: merging is the designed behaviour.

excerpts.quote: // Existing line keeps its original price and name snapshot. item.increaseQuantity(newItem.getQuantity());
Merging another quantity of the same product keeps that existing snapshot.

notes.title: How the menu handles a price with three decimals
notes.body:
**Key: "Please enter a non-negative amount with at most 2 decimal places, for example 19.99."**

createProduct reads the price through readMoney. readMoney parses the text and immediately calls DomainValues.money, which uses setScale(2, RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY). 0.004 cannot be scaled without rounding, so it throws; readMoney catches it, prints the hint and returns null, and the flow stops without creating anything. Piped input prints exactly this.

Why the others are wrong:
- **"Money must be greater than zero."**: the precision check fails first, inside readMoney, so the product code is never reached.
- **Stored at 0.00 or 0.01**: the reworked code rejects sub-cent amounts instead of rounding them silently (README).

excerpts.quote: try { normalized = value.setScale(2, RoundingMode.UNNECESSARY); }
Sub-cent amounts are rejected rather than rounded silently.

notes.title: Why loading uses restore instead of replaying edits
notes.body:
**Key: replay runs the user-command rules and stamps a new updatedAt; restore avoids both.**

A paid order on disk must come back with its items, discount and saved update time. Replaying would call addOrMergeItem and setDiscountAmount, which call ensureEditable and fail for PAID, and each successful call would touch updatedAt. Order.restore instead takes the complete item collection, copies it and validates the result once, preserving the saved timestamps.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Correct but slow**: replay would be wrong, not just slow, for any paid order.
- **Catalog products missing**: addOrMergeItem takes an OrderItem and does not look anything up in the catalog.
- **restore skips validation**: it validates duplicates, the discount and status-requires-items; damaged files are rejected, not repaired.

excerpts.quote: It does not call `addOrMergeItem` on a paid order, and it does not temporarily compare the discount to an empty subtotal.
// Restore the complete aggregate once, then validate the saved discount.

notes.title: What a corrupt snapshot does at startup
notes.body:
**Key: it prints the Startup stopped message and reason, then exits with status 0.**

FileDataStore.load wraps any failure as IllegalStateException("Failed to load order data: ..."). main catches the RuntimeException, prints "Startup stopped: " plus that message and "Existing data was not replaced. Repair a separate copy before retrying.", and returns. No System.exit call follows, so the JVM exits 0. Running the CLI on data/sample-corrupt shows exactly this.

Why the others are wrong:
- **System.exit(1)**: main has no exit call; a non-zero status is a practice exercise.
- **Empty data, then overwrite**: main returns before run, so nothing is ever saved.
- **Legacy fallback**: an existing snapshot is authoritative; a corrupt one is never replaced by older legacy files.

excerpts.quote: System.out.println("Startup stopped: " + error.getMessage());
a startup that refuses a corrupt file still exits with status 0

notes.title: Why three of the four legacy files are not enough
notes.body:
**Key: load fails with "Incomplete legacy dataset: all four files are required."**

With no snapshot, load counts which of customers.txt, products.txt, orders.txt and order_items.txt exist. Anything other than none or all four throws. A missing item file is not treated as "no items", because that would silently drop lines and could change totals and status rules. A probe with three files gets this error.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Orders loaded without items**: that is the silent data loss the check prevents.
- **Empty dataset**: an empty start happens only when none of the four files exists.
- **order_items.txt created later**: the app only ever writes oms.snapshot.txt.

excerpts.quote: if (present != 0 && present != files.length) throw new IOException("Incomplete legacy dataset: all four files are required.");
incomplete legacy data is rejected

notes.title: What happens when the save on exit fails
notes.body:
**Key: the app reports the failure and keeps the session open for a retry.**

Menu 13 calls exitApplication. If saveData returns false, it prints "Data could not be saved. Session stays open so you can retry." and returns true, which keeps the menu loop running. Nothing in memory is lost, so the user can fix the directory and choose 13 again. No automated test drives this branch, but running the CLI on a data path whose parent is a regular file reproduces it: choosing 13 prints the save error and that line, and the menu keeps reading input.

Why the others are wrong:
- **Exits and drops changes**: that would discard work silently; the method returns true to stay open.
- **Retries at next start**: nothing is queued for later; the data only exists in this session's memory.
- **Backup file**: there is no backup path in the save code.

excerpts.quote: System.out.println("Data could not be saved. Session stays open so you can retry."); return true;
A failed normal exit keeps the session open so the user can retry

notes.title: Going further: the worked change, the C# translation and the practice ladder
notes.body:
The later questions use three more lessons.

1. **astraupskill/03-WORKED-CHANGE.md** tells the story of one real defect and the redesign that followed: how loading used to build an order, what the new restore path does, how mutations and ownership were tightened, and why persistence moved to one snapshot file. Read it as a before-and-after comparison.
2. **astraupskill/08-THE-SAME-ORDER-IN-CSHARP.md** rebuilds the order in C# and EF Core: an entity sketch, the model configuration, how the same defect could reappear in EF, a table mapping each refusal to an HTTP status, and a two-test exercise.
3. **astraupskill/05-PRACTICE.md** is a ladder of exercises with runnable checks. Read the setup section first: how the checks run tells you what each one can prove.

The trace lab (07) is useful for its procedures; keep its collected answers closed until you have done the trace yourself.

excerpts.quote: These exercises extend the delivered code; none of them describes an existing feature.

notes.title: The zero discount came from the order in which an order was built
notes.body:
The old loader created the order with its saved discount first, while the item list was still empty, and the constructor recalculated totals straight away. Recalculation clamped any discount larger than the subtotal down to the subtotal, and the subtotal was zero at that moment, so the 5.00 discount became 0.00. The items were added afterwards, but the discount was already gone.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- The lesson says plainly this was not a formatting or scale problem.
- The multiplication was correct; the subtotal was simply computed before any lines existed.
- Field order in the file was not the cause; the loader read the discount and then threw it away.

excerpts.quote: it was an initialization-order defect
Because subtotal was temporarily zero, the discount became zero.

notes.title: Restore refuses impossible saved states instead of fixing them
notes.body:
The worked change describes two kinds of inconsistent saved data that the restore factory refuses: two lines for the same product, and a discount larger than the subtotal of all the saved lines. In both cases loading fails rather than quietly merging lines or shrinking the discount, because a silent repair would hide that the file is wrong. (The constructor behind restore also refuses a SUBMITTED, PAID or SHIPPED order with no lines, a rule the lesson does not list.)

Why the other answers are wrong:
- Duplicate lines are rejected, not merged, and a PAID order may keep a valid discount; paid status does not block reconstruction.
- Saved timestamps are kept as they are; nothing compares them or the status with a history.
- A DRAFT order may have no lines, and restore never compares a line's price with today's catalog.

excerpts.quote: rejects duplicate product lines
A saved discount greater than the final subtotal is rejected rather than silently repaired.

notes.title: A rejected change leaves the update time alone
notes.body:
Every mutation validates first and only then changes state and touches updatedAt. A discount with three decimals fails the precision check before assignment, so nothing about the order changes, including its update time. If a rejected request moved updatedAt, anyone reading the order would think an edit had succeeded.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- The order keeps no audit trail of attempts; updatedAt is not used for that.
- Not every call touches the order; only accepted changes do.
- The timestamp is never cleared; there is no manual-review flag.

The regression suite checks exactly this: an invalid discount leaves the amount and the timestamp unchanged.

excerpts.quote: Failed changes do not touch `updatedAt`, so a rejected request does not falsely look like a successful edit.

notes.title: Why one snapshot beats four separately written files
notes.body:
When customers, products, order metadata and items were each rewritten in their own file, a crash between two of those writes could leave, for example, new orders next to old items. The data on disk would then mix two generations that never existed together. One snapshot file, validated and written to a temporary sibling and then moved into place atomically, is either entirely old or entirely new.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- Speed is not the reason given.
- The record tags belong to the new single file; they did not force the change.
- Operating-system paths are not mentioned.

A corrupt snapshot now stops startup instead of falling back to the old files.

excerpts.quote: An interruption could combine different generations of data.

notes.title: A version column is new, and Total needs no clamp
notes.body:
The C# sketch adds a Version property marked [ConcurrencyCheck]. The Java order has no version yet; adding one is practice exercise 6. Total is simply Subtotal minus DiscountAmount, with no clamp at zero, because ApplyDiscount refuses any discount larger than the subtotal, just as the Java setDiscountAmount does. Since the bad state can never be created, there is nothing to clamp.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- The sketch uses an int Version, not a RowVersion, and relies on no CHECK constraint.
- EF does not round negative totals; there are none.
- CustomerId is not the new property, and no assumption about prices is made.

excerpts.quote: [ConcurrencyCheck] public int Version { get; private set; }
no clamp: ApplyDiscount refuses discount > Subtotal, as Order.java:101 does

notes.title: Owned lines and their captured prices
notes.body:
An owned type in EF Core has no identity of its own: an order line exists only as part of its order, the way the Java aggregate treats its items. Each line also captures the product name and unit price when it is added and never reads them from Product again, so later catalog price changes do not move existing orders.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- Lines are not shared between orders, and the price is not re-read from Product.
- Owned lines get no repository or id of their own, and nothing recomputes prices.
- The sketch maps lines to their own table, not to JSON, and the price is stored, not looked up.

excerpts.quote: owned: no identity outside its order
never re-read from Product

notes.title: How EF Core can recreate the empty-items trap, and how owned types avoid it
notes.body:
If order lines are a regular navigation and the query forgets Include, EF returns the order with an empty Items list. Applying a 5.00 discount then runs against a zero subtotal and throws, exactly the Java defect in a new costume. Owned types do not have this problem, because EF always loads them together with their owner, with or without Include. That makes the owned mapping the C# counterpart of Order.restore: one path that always yields the whole aggregate.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- The trap is not stale cache data.
- It is not lazy loading, and owned types are not loaded lazily.
- Split queries are not the cause, and owned lines here live in their own table.

excerpts.quote: EF Core loads owned types together with their owner on every query, without `Include`.

notes.title: Why a second CLI run proves the change was saved
notes.body:
Each practice check copies data/sample to a throwaway folder and starts the real CLI in a fresh JVM. Input is piped, so it ends with EOF, and the App saves when input ends. A check that runs the CLI a second time against the same copy therefore reads back what the first run saved: if the change shows up, it was persisted, not just held in memory.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- The real data folder is never used, and each run gets its own JVM.
- The checks drive the CLI, not OrderService directly.
- Nothing is replayed from a recording; the program really runs.

excerpts.quote: The checks drive the real CLI in a fresh JVM against a disposable copy of `data/sample`
a check that runs the CLI twice against the same copy also proves the change persisted

notes.title: An unknown status word leaks a Java class name
notes.body:
The delivered menu 11 hands the typed word straight to OrderStatus.valueOf. For an unknown word Java throws, and the CLI prints the exception text: No enum constant oms.domain.OrderStatus.TELEPORTED. That exposes an internal class name and tells the user nothing useful. Exercise 3 asks for explicit parsing at the boundary and a message starting Unknown status that lists the valid values.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- The CLI does not print an invalid menu option, and storing arbitrary statuses is not the goal.
- The order is not silently cancelled.
- The Unknown status message is the requested fix, not today's behaviour.

excerpts.quote: which leaks a Java class name to the user

notes.title: 422 or 409: a bad value versus a conflicting state
notes.body:
The C# sketch maps each refusal to one status so a client knows what to do next. A discount larger than the subtotal is a well-formed request whose value breaks a rule of the order: ApplyDiscount throws a DomainException and the API answers 422 Unprocessable Content. The fix is on the client side: send a smaller value. A content edit on an order whose status no longer allows edits is different: the value may be fine, but the order has moved on. That refusal comes from the status guard and maps to 409 Conflict, the same code the table uses for an out-of-graph transition and a stale save.

Why the other answers are wrong:
- The two refusals do not share a code; that is the point of the table.
- 400 is reserved for a body that fails validation, and 404 for an unknown product or customer.

excerpts.quote: `throw new DomainException(...)` from `ApplyDiscount` | 422
